source.title: Glomerulus Classification via an Improved GoogLeNet
source.authors: Xujing Yao; Xinyue Wang; YELl̇Z Karaca; Jia-Yong Xie; Shui-Hua Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study adds batch-normalization layers to GoogLeNet and reports classification performance, but it does not measure training error, training speed, or learning-rate tolerance as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-set classification metrics for GoogLeNet with and without batch normalization. These outcomes do not measure the claim versions’ training-error or training-speed outcomes. It also describes cited work on batch normalization; those cited results are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study uses batch normalization to improve a medical-image classifier and cites its optimization benefits, but reports testing-set accuracy and F1 scores rather than training speed, learning-rate tolerance, training error, or other outcomes named by V1–V6. Its Bayesian optimization trajectory measures hyperparameter search, not network convergence.
record.authors_conclusion: The authors conclude that their model accurately classifies three glomerulus categories, that adding BN and Bayesian optimization improves classification metrics, and that it outperforms published approaches. The record needs one correction: those published approaches reported their best results on their own datasets, rather than all being evaluated on this study's dataset.
record.recipe_differences: Medical-image classification using a pre-trained GoogLeNet feature extractor, added batch-normalization layers, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, and 5-fold cross validation; it does not test the claim’s convergence recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported testing-set accuracy differs between the model without BN layers and the final BN-Bayesian model; the latter also uses Bayesian optimization, so the comparison does not isolate BN’s effect.

fits_no_version.finding: Testing-set accuracy was 93.38±5.40% without added BN layers and 95.04±4.99% for the final GoogLeNet-BN-Bayesian model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The final model achieved higher reported held-out classification accuracy than the no-BN comparison on this glomerulus dataset.

record.problems: The reported comparison does not isolate the effect of batch normalization because the final model also uses Bayesian optimization. The paper reports testing-set accuracy, not training error or training speed.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results left out.

untested.parts: Training classification error under gradient training, including model-size effects and corrupted or random labels on CIFAR-10/100.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity shortcuts, and the specified initialization alternatives.
Effects of initialization on signal propagation, training speed, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature dynamics, and divergence.
Whether batch normalization accelerates training or permits higher learning rates; comparison with normalization-free Fixup training.

record.verdict_notes: The record's blanket claim that the BN comparison is confounded by Bayesian optimization is not established by the supplied text. Section V presents separate ablations without BN and without Bayesian optimization, suggesting each component is removed separately, although detailed matched training settings are not supplied. This does not change the verdict: held-out accuracy does not measure V6's training-speed or learning-rate claims.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, network size, CIFAR benchmarks, and corrupted or random labels.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks, spurious minima, and student width.
Depth effects on training error, residual shortcuts, plain tanh networks, and normalization-free residual networks.
Initialization comparisons, training speed, and trainable depth.
Training above stability limits, curvature, and divergence.
Training speed and tolerance of higher learning rates.
